articles.title: Scientists stunned by children's lung recovery in ultra low emission zone
articles.summary: Children's lung capacity caught up with their peers in less polluted areas once a clean air zone came in, a study shows.
articles.content:
Scientists say they have been "stunned" by how quickly young children's lungs began to recover and grow after pollution restrictions were brought in where they lived.

Researchers found that children in London whose lung growth had been stunted by pollution showed impressive improvements after the introduction of an Ultra Low Emission Zone (Ulez) in 2019 reduced emissions.

The study followed more than 3,400 primary school children in London and Luton and provides what scientists believe is the strongest evidence yet that local clean air zones could help reduce some of the harm caused by pollution during childhood.

But independent researchers caution that other factors must also be considered.

Air pollution can stunt the growth of young children's lungs leaving them at an increased risk of asthma, heart disease, diabetes and even premature death.

Children are also more vulnerable to pollution because their lungs and immune systems are still developing. And when outside, they tend to be closer to the ground and nearer sources of exhaust fumes, for example.

In 2020 Ella Adoo-Kissi-Debrah, a nine-year-old girl from London who died following an asthma attack in 2013, became the first person in the UK to have air pollution listed as a cause of death.

In the study, researchers recruited six to nine-year-olds attending primary schools in London's ultra low emission zone and followed the same children for five years, comparing them to similar children (in terms of socio-economic background, physical activity and ethnicity) in Luton.

Children in the study had annual lung function and capacity tests in the year before Ulez came in and for four years after.

Initial results showed children's lungs in London were smaller in capacity than those in Luton, which is less polluted than London but has a similar mix of pollutants.

At the end of the study the children's lung capacity reached near identical levels in both groups.

"While we would expect children's lungs to grow year on year, our results indicate that the London children's lung growth had accelerated during the four years to 'catch up' with the control group in Luton to reach similar levels of lung capacity," researchers say.

"I was absolutely stunned when I first saw the results," Prof Chris Griffiths, a senior author on the study, at Queen Mary University of London, told the BBC.

"The speed of catch up in lung capacity in the London group was surprising and impressive.

"This shows an ambitious clean air zone can drive pollution levels down, rapidly restoring children's stunted lung growth."

The main test measured how much air a child could forcibly breathe out in one second after a big breath in.

In practical terms the improvements could mean children in the London group could run as fast as the Luton group without getting out of breath or blow out of the same number of candles for example, Griffiths explained.

Another way of testing for lung capacity used in the study showed significant improvements too, though not to the same extent - implying there are still gains to be made.

Overall the proportion of children in London whose lung capacity was deemed "clinically impaired" (suggesting lung damage resulting in coughs or breathlessness) fell from 14% to 9%.

In Luton - where some smaller scale measures were put in place to tackle air pollution - the figures were 9% to 7%.

The team's measurements also showed the level of nitrogen dioxide children were exposed to fell faster in London than in Luton over this time.

Researchers say this is key as it likely demonstrates that the improved lung growth they saw was related to air quality improvements following the implementation of Ulez.

London's Ulez was first introduced in 2019 by Mayor Sadiq Khan in a bid to "clean up London's air". London had high levels of the harmful gas nitrogen dioxide which comes from motor vehicles.

Older, more polluting vehicles had to pay a daily charge to drive in central London. The measures were later expanded to cover the whole capital. While many supported the policy it provoked political opposition and protests.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant and measurable health improvement in children's lung capacity following the implementation of a clean air policy (Ultra Low Emission Zone) in London. This demonstrates a positive real-world impact on public health, especially for vulnerable children, with broad significance for urban pollution control policies worldwide. The study is detailed and focused on this single impactful topic.
articles.personality_title: London’s clean air zone helps children’s lungs recover quickly
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Air pollution can harm children’s lung growth, making it harder for them to breathe and increasing health risks. In 2019, London introduced the Ultra Low Emission Zone (Ulez) to reduce harmful vehicle emissions and improve air quality.

**What happened** – Scientists studied over 3,400 primary school children aged 6 to 9 in London and a less polluted town called Luton. They tested the children’s lung capacity every year from before Ulez started to four years after. At first, children in London had smaller lung capacity than those in Luton. But after the Ulez began, London children’s lung growth sped up and caught up with the Luton children.

**Impact** – This study shows for the first time that a local clean air zone like Ulez can quickly help children’s lungs recover from pollution damage. The number of London children with lung problems dropped from 14% to 9%. Improved lung capacity means children can run and play without getting out of breath as easily. It also reduces risks of diseases linked to poor lung health.

**What’s next step** – Researchers hope this evidence will encourage more cities to adopt clean air zones. They also want to study other factors that affect lung health and continue monitoring children’s lung growth to see if improvements last.

**One-sentence takeaway** – London’s Ultra Low Emission Zone helped children’s lungs grow stronger and healthier within just a few years by lowering pollution in the city.

articles.title: A revolutionary stem-cell therapy must proceed responsibly to achieve its full potential
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 18 August 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02524-2It is 20 years since induced pluripotent stem cells shook biomedicine. Public trust must be retained now that clinical trials are well under way.
articles.content:
It is 20 years since induced pluripotent stem cells shook biomedicine. Public trust must be retained now that clinical trials are well under way.

Shinya Yamanaka in 2012, the year he won a share of a Nobel prize.Credit: Aflo/Shutterstock

Shinya Yamanaka doesn’t see himself as a celebrity. But people do recognize the stem-cell researcher when he’s out for a run, often while training for a marathon, on the streets of Kyoto, Japan.

Many of them call out words of encouragement. Some tell him that they hope his research will lead to cures for family members who are battling severe illnesses. “I feel deeply humbled and grateful,” says Yamanaka, who splits his time between Kyoto University and the Gladstone Institutes in San Francisco, California.

Don’t rush promising stem-cell therapies

Some of the hoped-for cures could be nearing reality. It has been quite a wait — 20 years, in fact — since the paper1 that shook biomedical research and won Yamanaka a share of the 2012 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. In it, he and his colleague, Kazutoshi Takahashi, also at Kyoto University, unveiled a way to turn back time in adult mouse cells, erasing their identity and reprogramming them to an embryonic-like state — all by switching on just four genes.

That discovery opened up a possible way to treat disease. If those cells, called induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cells, could be coaxed to take on fresh identities, they might provide a source of healthy tissue, fashioned from a person’s own cells, that could repair diseased or damaged organs. Earlier this year, the first such therapies — one for Parkinson’s disease and the other for heart failure — received conditional approval in Japan2. Clinical trials of iPS-cell therapies are under way around the world.

The stem-cell field now stands at a turning point. As more therapies are rolled out, the goal of researchers, companies and regulators must be to ensure that these treatments are developed responsibly, and that they will be available to all who need them.

Japan’s big bet on stem-cell therapies might soon pay off with medical breakthroughs

Before the landmark 2006 paper in Cell, Yamanaka’s colleagues sometimes questioned the scientific path he was forging. They would tell him: “Those mouse cells may be interesting, but you should do something more closely related to human disease and human medicine,” as Yamanaka recalled during his Nobel prize lecture.

But his discovery was soon replicated in human cells3,4. After that, researchers had to work out how to induce iPS cells to acquire identities that could be useful for studying and treating disease.

Deepak Srivastava, a cardiologist and stem-cell researcher at the Gladstone Institutes, still remembers the joy he felt when he saw that his laboratory had finally generated heart cells from iPS cells. Even so, only about 1% of the iPS cells had adopted that new identity, he says. It would take more years of work before the lab could get 90% or more of their stem cells to become heart cells — enough for them to spontaneously beat in unison, generating waves in the culture medium.

Some medical applications were quick to follow. By deriving iPS cells from individuals with or without particular disorders, researchers were able to learn more about the molecular mechanisms underlying disease. Scientists can now use iPS cells to grow organoids, 3D masses of cells intended to emulate the structure and function of an organ. Pharmaceutical companies have incorporated iPS cells into their search for drugs against conditions such as motor neuron disease (amyotrophic lateral sclerosis).

How iPS cells changed the world

But before therapies based on iPS cells could be used in people, there was a major safety concern to address: stem cells that have not yet taken on a specific identity can seed tumours. Researchers needed to ensure that cells used for therapy had all been successfully reprogrammed to take on a new function, with no embryonic-like interlopers remaining that could give rise to cancer. This added to the development time for such therapies, says Srivastava.

Now, with those hurdles on the way to being overcome, it is time to test iPS-cell therapies. Many of the trials will report results over the next five years, covering therapies to treat conditions such as macular degeneration and diabetes. Researchers are continuing to collect data on the two therapies that received conditional approval in Japan after small, initial clinical studies to assess safety.

It is an exciting, but precarious, time for iPS-cell research. There is always a tremendous incentive to be the first in a burgeoning field, and iPS-cell therapy is at a stage when there are many potential firsts. These therapies could benefit very large numbers of people. But the field must proceed responsibly: moving too fast, without appropriate guidelines, increases the risk of harm. And one clinical trial that harms its participants could freeze the entire endeavour.

Clinical trials test the safety of stem-cell therapy for Parkinson’s disease

Making bespoke iPS-cell therapies from a person’s own cells is, in many cases, too slow and expensive to be practical. Researchers, including Yamanaka, have been working to develop off-the-shelf alternatives, in which iPS cells from one donor could be used to treat many people. This, along with improvements in how the cells are manufactured, could cut costs and make the treatments more accessible, as well as encouraging more companies to enter the field.

It might be hard, after a 20-year wait, to proceed slowly and steadily when treatments are finally in sight, but that is the nature of medical research. “Translational research is a marathon, not a sprint,” says Yamanaka, speaking from experience of races both literal and metaphorical. “Keeping patient benefit as your North Star will sustain you.”
articles.reasoning: The article highlights a major biomedical breakthrough—induced pluripotent stem cells (iPS cells)—that has opened new avenues for treating serious diseases like Parkinson's and heart failure. It discusses ongoing clinical trials and conditional approvals, emphasizing the potential for large-scale health benefits. The story provides substantial context about the scientific journey, challenges, and future prospects, underscoring responsible progress in a field with broad public impact.
articles.personality_title: Stem-cell breakthrough offers new hope for treating serious diseases
articles.personality_presentation:

articles.title: A therapy that “rewrites” childhood memories can ease fear of failure
articles.summary: Childhood criticism can leave people carrying a fear of failure long into adulthood, but new research suggests those emotional patterns may be surprisingly flexible. Young adults who revisited painful memories through imagery-based therapy showed lasting reductions in fear, guilt, sadness, and stress.
articles.content:
Certain imagery-based psychotherapy techniques may help reduce fear of failure connected to painful childhood experiences, according to research from scientists at SWPS University and the Nencki Institute of Experimental Biology. The findings were published in the journal Frontiers in Psychology.

Difficult experiences early in life, including criticism, neglect, or severe reactions from caregivers, can influence emotional well-being and quality of life years later. How adults respond when a child makes a mistake may be especially important in shaping future patterns of thought and emotion. In some cases, those experiences can contribute to a fear of failure rooted in the belief that mistakes make a person less worthy in the eyes of others.

Researchers from the Poznań-based Laboratory of Affective Neuroscience at the Institute of Psychology, SWPS University, and the Laboratory of Brain Imaging at the Nencki Institute of Experimental Biology in Warsaw set out to determine whether imagery-based psychotherapy could reduce the ongoing effects of these painful memories on everyday life.

Testing Whether Memory Work Can Create Lasting Change

The randomized, controlled clinical trial included 180 young adults (between 18 and 35 years of age) who experienced fear of failure. During a two-week period, participants took part in four therapy sessions focused on difficult childhood memories involving criticism.

One group used the Imagery Exposure (IE) technique. Participants were asked to recall situations that had triggered fear or anxiety (the active control group).

A second group received Imagery Rescripting (ImRs), a technique designed to change the way a memory unfolds in the imagination. Participants brought a distressing experience to mind and then imagined a "defender" (e.g., a therapist) entering the scene, confronting the person delivering the criticism, and offering support to the child.

The third group used the same therapeutic approach, but with a 10-minute delay procedure (ImRs-DSR). Researchers designed this delay to interfere with the memory trace associated with the critical experience, potentially strengthening the intervention's effects.

Participants completed questionnaires and interviews, while researchers also tracked physiological measures. Follow-up assessments took place three and six months later.

Fear, Guilt, and Stress Declined

All of the imagery-based approaches produced a significant and lasting reduction in fear of failure. Participants also reported lower levels of negative emotions, including sadness and guilt.

Their bodies appeared to respond differently as well. Physiological reactions to memories of criticism decreased, indicating that recalling distressing experiences no longer triggered the same level of intense stress. These improvements remained evident during follow-ups at three and six months, suggesting that the psychological effects were stable over time.

"The study shows that it is possible to reduce the intensity of negative emotions and arousal associated with memories of childhood criticism. Properly selected techniques can influence how these memories are experienced, making them less burdensome," says study co-author Julia Bączek, a psychologist from the Laboratory of Affective Neuroscience at the Institute of Psychology, SWPS University.

Why Surprise May Matter

The researchers found that imagery rescripting worked especially well when it produced a moment of surprise. They linked this effect to prediction error, which occurs when there is a mismatch between what someone expects and what actually happens.

That unexpected difference may help loosen established emotional patterns and make it easier for the mind to replace old, painful responses with new ones.

"We have shown that a crucial part of imagery-based therapy is creating a discrepancy between what the patient expects and what actually happens in the new memory. It is this surprise that paves the way for a lasting therapeutic change," says study co-author Stanisław Karkosz, a cognitive scientist from the Laboratory of Affective Neuroscience at the Institute of Psychology, SWPS University.

Painful Memories Do Not Have to Stay Emotionally Fixed

The findings suggest that imagery-based techniques can change how people respond to current challenges by allowing them to "write" new, safe endings to painful experiences from the past.

The results also indicate that difficult memories (including those related to failure) do not necessarily have to be experienced in the same emotional way forever. Julia Bączek emphasizes that past experiences can be processed differently over time, rather than remaining fixed and unchangeable.
articles.reasoning: This article reports on a significant, well-researched psychotherapy breakthrough that helps reduce fear of failure rooted in childhood criticism. The study demonstrates lasting emotional and physiological improvements in young adults, indicating a meaningful positive impact on mental health and quality of life for a broad population. The detailed clinical trial and follow-up data provide substantial context and evidence of the therapy's effectiveness.
articles.personality_title: New therapy helps reduce fear of failure linked to childhood criticism
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Childhood experiences, especially criticism from caregivers, can cause people to fear failure even as adults. This fear can make them feel less worthy and affect their emotions and daily life.

**What happened** – Scientists in Poland tested a special therapy called imagery-based psychotherapy on 180 young adults aged 18 to 35. Over two weeks, participants took part in four sessions where they recalled painful childhood memories. Some used a method called Imagery Rescripting, which asks them to imagine someone supporting the child in the memory and changing the story to be more positive.

**Impact** – The therapy helped reduce fear of failure, sadness, guilt, and stress. Participants showed fewer strong emotional and physical reactions when thinking about their childhood criticism. These improvements lasted for at least six months after the therapy ended, showing that the changes were stable.

**What's next step** – Researchers want to explore how the feeling of surprise during therapy helps change emotional patterns. They also hope to apply this therapy to help more people who struggle with negative memories and fears from childhood.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Imagery-based therapy can help change painful childhood memories and reduce fear of failure, improving emotional well-being over time.
articles.personality_title_fr: Une nouvelle thérapie réduit la peur de l’échec liée aux critiques infantiles
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les expériences d’enfance, notamment les critiques des parents, peuvent provoquer une peur de l’échec à l’âge adulte. Cette peur peut faire sentir moins digne une personne et affecter ses émotions et sa vie quotidienne.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Des chercheurs polonais ont testé une thérapie appelée psychothérapie basée sur l’imagerie auprès de 180 jeunes adultes de 18 à 35 ans. Pendant deux semaines, les participants ont suivi quatre séances où ils revivaient des souvenirs douloureux d’enfance. Certains ont utilisé la technique de remaniement par l’imagerie, qui consiste à imaginer une personne soutenant l’enfant dans le souvenir et changeant l’histoire en quelque chose de plus positif.

**Impact** – La thérapie a réduit la peur de l’échec, la tristesse, la culpabilité et le stress. Les participants ont montré moins de réactions émotionnelles et physiques fortes en pensant à leurs critiques d’enfance. Ces améliorations ont duré au moins six mois après la fin de la thérapie, montrant que les changements étaient stables.

**Prochaine étape** – Les chercheurs veulent comprendre comment la surprise ressentie pendant la thérapie aide à changer les schémas émotionnels. Ils espèrent aussi utiliser cette thérapie pour aider davantage de personnes ayant des souvenirs négatifs et des peurs liées à l’enfance.

**Résumé en une phrase** – La thérapie basée sur l’imagerie peut modifier les souvenirs douloureux d’enfance et réduire la peur de l’échec, améliorant ainsi le bien-être émotionnel sur le long terme.
articles.personality_title_es: Nueva terapia reduce el miedo al fracaso ligado a críticas infantiles
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Las experiencias de la infancia, especialmente las críticas de los cuidadores, pueden causar miedo al fracaso en la adultez. Este miedo puede hacer que las personas se sientan menos valiosas y afectar sus emociones y vida diaria.

**Qué pasó** – Científicos en Polonia probaron una terapia llamada psicoterapia basada en imágenes con 180 adultos jóvenes entre 18 y 35 años. Durante dos semanas, los participantes tuvieron cuatro sesiones donde recordaron recuerdos dolorosos de la infancia. Algunos usaron una técnica llamada reescritura por imágenes, que les pide imaginar a alguien apoyando al niño en el recuerdo y cambiando la historia a algo más positivo.

**Impacto** – La terapia ayudó a reducir el miedo al fracaso, la tristeza, la culpa y el estrés. Los participantes mostraron menos reacciones emocionales y físicas intensas al pensar en las críticas de su infancia. Estas mejoras duraron al menos seis meses después de la terapia, mostrando que los cambios fueron estables.

**Próximo paso** – Los investigadores quieren estudiar cómo la sorpresa durante la terapia ayuda a cambiar patrones emocionales. También esperan aplicar esta terapia para ayudar a más personas con recuerdos negativos y miedos de la infancia.

**Conclusión en una frase** – La terapia basada en imágenes puede cambiar recuerdos dolorosos de la infancia y reducir el miedo al fracaso, mejorando el bienestar emocional a largo plazo.

articles.title: Postbiotic could reduce the risk of brain damage after a concussion
articles.summary: Giving mice a byproduct produced by gut bacteria reduced their risk of severe brain damage and cognitive difficulties after a traumatic brain injury
articles.content:
Our gut microbiota leave behind helpful postbiotics after digestion Redjina Ph/Getty Images

A postbiotic could reduce the risk of damage after a traumatic brain injury, such as a concussion. Mice that had traumatic brain injuries experienced less damage and performed better on cognitive tests if they were given a postbiotic – a byproduct produced when gut bacteria digest food – before injury. This suggests the postbiotic could be given preventatively to people who are particularly at risk of traumatic brain injuries, such as military personnel.

The gut microbiome is known to influence the brain, and vice versa. Research suggests it may help modulate the effects of traumatic brain injuries, which affect tens of millions of people worldwide each year.

The molecule indole-3-propionic acid (IPA) is produced when gut bacteria break down tryptophan, an amino acid in food such as meat, fish and eggs. Previous studies have linked lower IPA to worse outcomes after subarachnoid haemorrhage, a rare type of stroke that causes bleeding in the brain, and in people with Alzheimer’s disease.

Advertisement

Now, Yan Qu at the Air Force Medical University in Shaanxi, China, and his colleagues have measured it in blood samples from 106 people with traumatic brain injuries. They found that higher levels were associated with less swelling around brain lesions and better neurological outcomes six months later.

Next, the researchers – who didn’t respond to a request for an interview – induced a brain injury in mice that had been given either IPA or a control solution every day for two weeks. They found that the treated mice had less brain swelling, neuronal death and tissue damage than the control group three days later. They also performed better on tests of movement, learning and memory up to 14 days after their injury.

Free newsletter Sign up to Health Check Sign up to newsletter

Traumatic brain injuries cause a series of neurological changes that occur in phases. One phase involves enzymes attacking mitochondrial membranes, causing them to disintegrate, which leads to oxidative damage. This then causes violently reactive compounds, which are usually sequestered inside mitochondria, to leak out, ultimately leading to neuroinflammation and cell death.

Through a series of imaging and cell experiments, the researchers found that IPA appeared to protect the mitochondria inside the mice’s astrocytes – cells that provide energy and support to neurons, but can become reactive and release inflammatory signals after an injury.

The team traced this protective effect to IPA activating the so-called aryl hydrocarbon receptor in astrocytes, preserving their mitochondria’s function, while also suppressing immune responses linked to inflammation.

“This new study significantly advances the field by identifying a detailed mechanism through which IPA preserves astrocytic mitochondrial [regulation] after traumatic brain injury,” says Miguel Pappolla at the University of Texas Medical Branch in Galveston, whose team first reported IPA’s neuroprotective properties in 1999.

But the mice were given IPA before their brain injury. “This is prophylaxis, not therapy,” says Federico Rey at the University of Wisconsin–Madison. “No one can pre-dose a car crash.” He notes, however, that this approach could be explored in people at risk of repeated head impacts, such as contact-sport athletes or military personnel.

Two advantages of IPA, which isn’t yet available as a supplement, are that it is an inexpensive compound and can be taken orally, says Rey. However, doses may have to be tailored depending on the level of IPA a person already has from their microbiome, say Rey and Sonia Villapol at Houston Methodist Scholars in Texas. “Patients differ in injury severity and location, age, sex, diet, medications, antibiotics, intensive-care exposures and pre-existing microbiome composition,” says Villapol.

Qu and his colleagues write in their paper that they are planning to further study the link between IPA and traumatic brain injury outcomes in people, and that future studies should test the effects of IPA administration after an injury.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific discovery that a postbiotic compound (IPA) can reduce brain damage and improve cognitive outcomes after traumatic brain injury, demonstrated in animal models and supported by human data. This has broad potential impact for millions affected by brain injuries worldwide, including military personnel and athletes, and suggests a new preventive approach with a clear biological mechanism and plans for further research.
articles.personality_title: Postbiotic compound shows promise in reducing brain damage after concussion
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Traumatic brain injuries, like concussions, affect millions of people worldwide each year. Scientists are exploring new ways to protect the brain and improve recovery, especially for those at high risk such as athletes and military personnel.

**What happened** – Researchers in China studied a molecule called indole-3-propionic acid (IPA), a byproduct made by gut bacteria when they digest food. They found that higher IPA levels in people with brain injuries were linked to less brain swelling and better recovery after six months. In lab tests, mice given IPA daily before a brain injury had less brain damage and performed better in learning and memory tests compared to mice that did not get IPA.

**Impact** – This study is important because it shows, for the first time, how IPA helps protect brain cells by supporting tiny structures called mitochondria in brain support cells. These mitochondria usually get damaged after injury, causing inflammation and cell death. IPA activates a receptor that keeps mitochondria working and reduces harmful inflammation. This discovery offers a new way to prevent brain damage before injury occurs.

**What's next step** – The researchers plan to study how IPA affects people after brain injuries and test if giving IPA after an injury can help recovery. While IPA is not yet available as a supplement, it is inexpensive and can be taken by mouth, making it a possible future treatment for people at risk of repeated head injuries.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A natural compound made by gut bacteria may protect the brain from damage after injury by keeping brain cells healthy and reducing inflammation.
articles.personality_title_fr: Un postbiotique pourrait réduire les dommages cérébraux après une commotion
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les traumatismes crâniens, comme les commotions, touchent des millions de personnes chaque année dans le monde. Les scientifiques cherchent de nouvelles façons de protéger le cerveau et d'améliorer la récupération, surtout pour les personnes à risque comme les sportifs et les militaires.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Des chercheurs en Chine ont étudié une molécule appelée acide indole-3-propionique (IPA), un sous-produit fabriqué par les bactéries intestinales lors de la digestion. Ils ont découvert que des niveaux plus élevés d’IPA chez des personnes blessées au cerveau étaient liés à moins de gonflement cérébral et une meilleure récupération au bout de six mois. En laboratoire, des souris ayant reçu de l’IPA quotidiennement avant une blessure cérébrale présentaient moins de dégâts et réussissaient mieux des tests d’apprentissage et de mémoire que celles qui n’en avaient pas reçu.

**Impact** – Cette étude est importante car elle montre, pour la première fois, comment l’IPA aide à protéger les cellules du cerveau en soutenant les mitochondries, de petites structures dans les cellules de soutien cérébral. Ces mitochondries sont généralement endommagées après une blessure, ce qui cause inflammation et mort cellulaire. L’IPA active un récepteur qui maintient les mitochondries en fonctionnement et réduit l’inflammation nocive. Cette découverte offre une nouvelle façon de prévenir les dommages cérébraux avant une blessure.

**Prochaines étapes** – Les chercheurs prévoient d’étudier comment l’IPA agit chez les personnes après une blessure cérébrale et tester si l’administration d’IPA après la blessure peut aider à la récupération. Bien que l’IPA ne soit pas encore disponible en complément, il est peu coûteux et peut être pris par voie orale, ce qui en fait un traitement possible pour les personnes exposées à des blessures répétées.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Un composé naturel produit par les bactéries intestinales pourrait protéger le cerveau des dommages après une blessure en maintenant les cellules cérébrales en bonne santé et en réduisant l’inflammation.
articles.personality_title_es: Un postbiótico podría reducir el daño cerebral tras una conmoción
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Las lesiones cerebrales traumáticas, como las conmociones, afectan a millones de personas cada año en todo el mundo. Los científicos buscan nuevas formas de proteger el cerebro y mejorar la recuperación, especialmente en personas con alto riesgo como deportistas y militares.

**Qué pasó** – Investigadores en China estudiaron una molécula llamada ácido indol-3-propiónico (IPA), un subproducto producido por las bacterias intestinales al digerir los alimentos. Encontraron que niveles más altos de IPA en personas con lesiones cerebrales se relacionaban con menos inflamación cerebral y mejor recuperación después de seis meses. En experimentos con ratones, aquellos que recibieron IPA diariamente antes de una lesión cerebral tuvieron menos daño y mejor desempeño en pruebas de aprendizaje y memoria que los que no recibieron IPA.

**Impacto** – Este estudio es importante porque muestra, por primera vez, cómo el IPA ayuda a proteger las células del cerebro apoyando las mitocondrias, pequeñas estructuras en las células de soporte cerebral. Estas mitocondrias suelen dañarse tras una lesión, causando inflamación y muerte celular. El IPA activa un receptor que mantiene las mitocondrias funcionando y reduce la inflamación dañina. Este descubrimiento ofrece una nueva forma de prevenir el daño cerebral antes de una lesión.

**Próximo paso** – Los investigadores planean estudiar cómo el IPA afecta a las personas después de una lesión cerebral y probar si administrar IPA después de la lesión puede ayudar a la recuperación. Aunque el IPA aún no está disponible como suplemento, es barato y se puede tomar por vía oral, lo que lo convierte en un posible tratamiento futuro para personas con riesgo de lesiones repetidas.

**Frase clave** – Un compuesto natural producido por bacterias intestinales podría proteger el cerebro del daño tras una lesión manteniendo las células cerebrales saludables y reduciendo la inflamación.
